extracted: The highlights say immunoassays have many weaknesses that can result in false-positive and false-negative results, and that testing for designer drugs (synthetic cathinones and cannabinoids) is challenging because the compounds keep changing and new ones keep appearing. Screens are immunoassays, run in a laboratory or on site as point-of-care tests, which use antibodies to detect drug metabolites or classes of drug metabolites; point-of-care tests have the same limitations as laboratory immunoassays and should be used only to screen. All initial immunoassay results are presumptive; GC-MS, the criterion standard for confirmation, identifies specific molecular structures and quantifies what is present, but it is time-consuming and costly and is therefore reserved for confirming positive screens; LC-MS/MS is an alternative.

extracted: Urine drug tests may not detect all opioids equally. Most conventional opiate immunoassays use morphine as the single calibrator that sets the line between a positive and a negative result; because the antibodies cross-react little with oxycodone, hydrocodone, hydromorphone and oxymorphone, false negatives are a risk, and more advanced immunoassays or LC-MS/MS show higher specificity and can maximize detection of these. Fentanyl, methadone and buprenorphine differ in chemical structure from morphine, so commonly marketed morphine-specific immunoassays do not react to them; they require immunoassays specific for these compounds or LC-MS/MS. Some laboratories do not routinely test for semisynthetic or synthetic opioids in a standard opioid test unless specially requested, and clinicians are told to know their laboratory's immunoassays and its access to LC-MS/MS before testing. GC-MS, LC-MS/MS and other procedures to measure tramadol and its metabolites in urine have been developed (p. 11).

extracted: For US federal and Department of Transportation workplace testing the opiate cutoff is 2000 ng/mL; it was raised from 300 ng/mL of morphine in 1998 to limit the many positives from poppy seeds and prescription opiates. This high cutoff can give negative results that make recent opioid use hard to interpret, especially when testing for synthetic and semisynthetic opioids; clinicians monitoring prescribed opioids may need the lower 300 ng/mL threshold and should know their laboratory's cutoff. The most common reasons for false-negative opioid results are using the wrong test for the specific opioid and too little opioid in the urine.

source_read: PDF PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Moeller_2017_ClinicalInterpretationUrineDrugTests.pdf (article in press, Mayo Clin Proc 2017, PDF pp. 1–23, which differ from the version of record), text pages 1–17 and the cited reference entries read; PDF pp. 2, 4–7, 9–11 and 15–16 checked on 150-dpi renderings
extracted: Benzodiazepine immunoassays are hard to interpret partly because they cannot tell individual benzodiazepines apart. Two significant limitations may lead to false negatives: the immunoassays cannot detect conjugated metabolites, and the cutoffs are high. Most are designed to detect the free (unconjugated) forms of oxazepam or nordiazepam, metabolites shared by several benzodiazepines (for example diazepam, chlordiazepoxide and temazepam); many benzodiazepines, for example lorazepam and alprazolam, are excreted as glucuronide conjugates and are not detected by most immunoassays unless the urine is first hydrolysed with beta-glucuronidase, which most laboratories do not do. Clonazepam, reduced mainly to 7-aminoclonazepam and not converted to oxazepam, may give a false negative and does not cross-react well. Cutoffs of 200 or 300 ng/mL were first set on the basis of older benzodiazepines (diazepam, oxazepam, flurazepam) and are often too high for lorazepam, alprazolam and triazolam; Fraser and Meatherall found that lowering the cutoff for alprazolam and triazolam to 100 ng/mL, with enzyme hydrolysis, increased positive results, and West et al. recommended 40 ng/mL to detect 7-aminoclonazepam.

extracted: Nabilone, a prescribed synthetic cannabinoid, tests negative for THC because of its distinct metabolites (p. 7). Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected as cannabis on urine drug tests (p. 15). Several immunoassays and point-of-care tests have been made for synthetic cannabinoids, but new compounds keep being developed, which makes testing for specific ones in urine difficult; little or no parent drug reaches urine; most assays are designed to detect metabolites of JWH-018 and JWH-073, with broader detection where other compounds share their metabolic pathway, and the compound taken is hard to identify (pp. 15–16). There is no accepted cutoff (assays range from 5 to 25 ng/mL). In Barnes et al., an ELISA kit for JWH-018 metabolites was tested against 73 synthetic cannabinoids: metabolites of several others cross-reacted significantly; raising the cutoff from 5 to 10 µg/L increased false-negative results by 12% (of what is not stated); and the test was limited in detecting newer compounds such as PB-22, RCS-4, RCS-8, XRL-11 and AKB48 (p. 16).
